extracted.intended_audience: NLP/ML researchers and practitioners developing or using automatic creativity evaluation for text (LLM evaluators, dataset creators, annotators, model trainers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, collecting, and training evaluators and datasets for automatic assessment of textual creativity (LLM-based and human-annotated), with emphasis on pairwise comparisons, annotator consensus, and data selection for model alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual conditioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual conditioning is crucial for accurate creativity assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should condition judgments on the prompt/context; creativity must be assessed relative to the instruction or prompt that produced the response rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise-comparison evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a pairwise-comparison framework for evaluating textual creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame creativity evaluation as pairwise comparisons because this aligns with training algorithms (e.g., DPO, reward models), produces clearer relative judgments, and is directly applicable for model alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus-driven aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Model shared human judgment using pairwise comparisons and consensus-driven aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate multiple annotator pairwise judgments to form a reproducible collective measure of creativity; consensus mitigates individual subjectivity while aiming to reflect shared intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborate with annotators from diverse backgrounds to ensure robust, collective understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit annotators with varied backgrounds to capture broader cultural/perspective variation and ensure the evaluation framework reflects a robust, collective human judgment rather than idiosyncratic tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusivity of creativity types
rubrics_metrics.description: Support multiple forms of creativity, including surprising, offbeat, or subversive responses, provided they are meaningful and novel to the prompt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluation should not equate creativity with conformity or majority taste; include and allow nonconventional responses as long as they are relevant and novel with respect to the prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty plus usefulness/meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity judgments should combine novelty with usefulness/meaningfulness to the prompt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in psychological findings, annotators should reward responses that are both novel and meaningful/useful in the prompt context (novelty alone is insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolute score scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute score-based evaluation is unreliable due to annotator inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute 1–5 scales produce substantial inter-annotator divergence (examples show up to ~1.02 point differences) and are hard to keep consistent across contexts; therefore prefer relative/pairwise judgments for large-scale alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct pair construction (not via derived absolute scores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct preference pairs directly through pairwise comparison rather than deriving them from absolute scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pairs constructed directly are more reliable and provide clearer training signals for ranking/training (derived pairs from absolute scores tend to be less reliable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Win rate as an efficient ranking metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Use win rate from pairwise comparisons to rank model responses efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To quickly rank responses, use any model response as a reference and compute win rates across pairwise comparisons; this incurs minimal computational overhead while providing robust relative rankings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine human and synthetic data in training evaluators
rubrics_metrics.description: Training robust creativity evaluators requires combining both human and synthetic data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical results highlight the essential role of mixing human annotations with synthetic (model-generated) data to improve evaluator robustness and out-of-distribution generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity-aware data selection and balanced difficulty mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Use creativity-aware data selection and a balanced mixture of difficulty levels in training data (e.g., include hard samples as rejections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting data with awareness of creativity difficulty and balancing easy/hard samples (example: DPO-70E30H uses 30% hard samples as rejections) boosts performance; treating all easy samples as rejections (DPO-100E) yields only marginal improvement, so maintain a clear distinction between chosen and rejected examples and a balanced mixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear distinction between chosen and rejected examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a clear distinction between chosen and rejected examples in training data to learn creativity signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training methods benefit from an explicit, discernible separation between preferred (chosen) and non-preferred (rejected) responses; ambiguous or noisy distinctions harm learning of creative preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate evaluator into generation pipelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate creativity evaluators (e.g., CrEval) into generation pipelines to boost LLM creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical application: use the trained evaluator as part of generation/selection/optimization loops to improve model creative outputs (e.g., via reranking or reward-based fine-tuning).
